desc:
The string expr is built from integer literals and calls of three functions: min(...), max(...) and sum(...). Every call has one or more arguments separated by commas, and each argument is either an integer literal or another call. A literal may be negative (-5). There are no spaces. The whole string is either one call or one literal.

min and max return the smallest and the largest of their arguments, sum returns their sum. Evaluate the expression and return its value.

Example: max(3,min(8,-2),sum(1,2,3)) evaluates the arguments to 3, -2 and 6, so the result is 6.
constraints: expr is valid: function names are exactly min, max or sum; every call has at least one argument
Literals are integers without leading zeros and without a '+' sign, e.g. 0, 15, -7
Calls can be nested up to 2,000 levels deep
Every literal and the result of every call (including partial sums) has absolute value at most 2<sup>31</sup> - 1
hints: A call can contain other calls, so the evaluation is naturally nested: finish the innermost call first.
Keep a stack with one entry per call that has been opened but not yet closed. Each entry stores the function name and the list of argument values collected so far.

On a name followed by ( push [name, []]. On a number append it to the top entry's list. On ) pop the top entry, reduce its list with the function, and append the result to the new top entry (or return it if the stack is empty). Do not forget that the whole expression may be just a number.
editorial: Evaluating from the inside out is exactly what a stack does. Scan the string once. When a function name is read, skip the following ( and push a frame holding the name and an empty list of argument values. Commas can simply be skipped, because numbers are recognised by their digits and sign.

A number (optionally starting with -) is converted and appended to the argument list of the top frame; if there is no frame the whole expression is that number. On ) the top frame is complete: apply min, max or sum to its list. If the stack is now empty this is the final answer, otherwise the result is appended to the argument list of the new top frame, exactly as if it had been written as a literal.

Each character is read once and each value is stored in one list, so the time is O(n); the stack depth equals the nesting depth, which is why this approach also works for 2,000 levels where a recursive parser might hit the recursion limit.
